title: Cutting Degrees that Dont Add Value
author: Michael B. Horn
summary: Horn argues that as American higher education faces demographic decline, many universities will respond with dramatic program cuts rather than full closures. He cites Syracuse closing 93 of 460 academic programs (including 55 with zero majors) and University of North Texas consolidating 70+ programs. About 60 colleges close each year already (over 1.5% annually), before the 20-year demographic decline fully hits. But Horn frames cutting as opportunity: an explicit chance to prioritize a college's mission and the programs that produce most value for students and the surrounding region. The piece is anchored on his Future U. interview with UNT President Harrison Keller (formerly Texas's higher-ed commissioner), who runs three quantitative tests on programs: time-to-value (how quickly do students break even on their investment, including opportunity cost?), contribution margin (how expensive is the program for the institution to offer?), and demand (from students and regional employers). At UNT the bachelor's-degree average time-to-value is six years, with some programs at three or four and about a dozen programs at more than ten — the latter is where attention focuses, and where some teach-out decisions get made. Keller addresses high-social-value-but-low-pay programs (social work) and the specific levers available to make them viable. The closing reflection is on what high-value liberal arts could look like if institutions shifted how they teach them rather than treating them as inherited overhead.
points: Many universities will respond to demographic decline with dramatic program cuts rather than full closures (Syracuse cut 93 of 460 programs, UNT 70+); about 60 colleges already close each year, before the 20-year demographic decline fully hits.

Cutting can be opportunity rather than just defense: an explicit chance to focus on the programs producing most value for students and the surrounding region, rather than maintaining everything by inertia.

UNT President Harrison Keller's three-question framework: time-to-value (how quickly do students break even, including opportunity cost?), contribution margin (how expensive is it for the school to offer?), demand (from students and regional employers?).

At UNT the bachelor's-degree average time-to-value is six years, with some programs at three or four and about a dozen at more than ten — where attention focuses and some teach-out decisions get made.
High-social-value-but-low-pay programs (e.g., social work) need explicit policy and funding levers to remain viable when measured against the same time-to-value math.
quotes: It's quite possible that many schools won't close or merge — they'll make dramatic cuts instead. Witness Syracuse University closing 93 of its 460 academic programs (including 55 programs where zero students were majoring). Or the University of North Texas announcing plans to cut or consolidate over 70 of its programs.
About 60 colleges are closing each year. That's over 1.5% of all colleges closing — each year — even before the impact of the demographic decline of the next 20 years fully materializes.
Yet cutting isn't all doom and gloom. It can be a big opportunity to prioritize and focus on a college's mission and the programs that produce the most value for students and the surrounding region.

The average for a bachelor's degree at UNT is six years. That means all in, your total investment in your undergraduate program including opportunity costs and that you would be net positive within six years. We've got some programs, it's three or four. We have about a dozen undergraduate programs when you look into that data, that it can be more than ten years.

So then that helps us know where we need to focus our attention in either improving those programs, or in some cases we have to make hard decisions that we're gonna teach these out. We've got to spin these down.

You can't be all things to all people, so there are things that make sense for UNT to do, and there are things that maybe we're not the best platform for.” Archived from Michael B. Horn Substack on May 1, 2026 by Tim.
